title: Bad Timing
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 31 of 40
content:
Our reservation lasted four minutes.

I'd spent two weeks finding a little restaurant in Beach City where the tables were far enough apart for conversation and the menu didn't require us to pretend we understood French. Greg had found a shirt without a guitar slogan on it.

He arrived early.

That should have been our first warning.

We were barely seated when his phone rang. He looked at the screen, sighed, and answered.

"Steven?"

I watched his expression change.

"Is everybody okay?"

A pause.

"Okay. I'm coming."

He hung up and looked at me.

"There's a situation by the boardwalk. Three Gems, something cracked, nobody hurt so far. Steven asked if I could bring the van."

I stared at the untouched water glasses.

"Right."

"I'm sorry."

"I know."

He stood, then stopped.

"Do you want to come?"

I considered. Being invited was not the same as being required.

"Yes. But I'm allowed to be disappointed."

He gave me a bewildered smile.

"Absolutely."

We apologized to the server, paid for the drinks, and left. Greg promised we'd come back when he could keep the reservation. He didn't ask the restaurant to hold a table indefinitely because his family had a crisis.

The boardwalk was chaos.

A section of decorative railing had cracked, one parking meter was bent almost in half, and the windshield of a parked car had a long white fracture running from one corner to the other. Garnet, Pearl and Amethyst were arguing about where to move a damaged piece of Gem equipment. Steven was trying to keep passersby away from the area.

Greg pulled into a legal space and stopped.

"What's the plan?" he asked.

Pearl explained that they needed a vehicle to transport the damaged equipment to a safer location. Greg looked at the windshield and then at the distance to the van.

"I can help with a trip," he said. "Not until we know it can be moved without hurting anyone."

Garnet nodded.

We set up a temporary barrier while Steven spoke with the local staff about closing the damaged walkway. Amethyst found a way to make the work sound like a carnival game. Nobody was amused except Greg.

I was annoyed enough to laugh anyway.

When the equipment had been secured, Greg helped load it using the method Pearl demonstrated. I stayed by the railing and kept people from wandering through the marked area. It took longer than anybody wanted. Rain began before we finished.

By the time the van was free, the restaurant had closed.

Greg stared at the dark storefront from across the street.

"That's one way to make a date memorable."

I folded my arms.

"Greg."

He looked at me.

"I am not angry that Steven needed help," I said. "I am upset that every time something goes wrong, you act as though the only correct feeling is gratitude that nothing worse happened."

His smile fell.

"I just don't want you to be mad at me."

"I'm allowed to be sad we missed something we'd planned."

He rubbed the back of his neck.

"I was sad too."

"Then why didn't you say it?"

"Because if I say it, I feel selfish. Like I'm choosing dinner over family."

I leaned against the van.

"Those aren't our only two choices."

He looked at the street.

"Steven matters to me."

"I know."

"So do you."

"I know that too."

"And sometimes the timing is terrible."

"Yes."

We stood under the awning until the rain softened. I wasn't going to turn the emergency into a test of whether he loved me, but neither of us could keep using jokes to hide what needed saying.

"Could we make a new plan?" he asked.

"Yes. A real one."

"Tomorrow evening?"

"I'm at Moonroot tomorrow. Saturday?"

He checked his calendar.

"Saturday works. I'll make the reservation, and if something happens I'll tell you as early as I can."

"Good."

He reached for my hand.

"Can I be disappointed about tonight now?"

"You're practically required."

He laughed, relieved.

We ate noodles in the van. The seats smelled of rain and the paper cartons balanced precariously between us. Greg told me about the first time he'd tried to take someone on a date and arrived with the wrong address. I told him about a Lanternweald meeting where the bridge committee had spent an hour arguing over a sign nobody could read.

"Maybe we should hire a scheduling wizard," he said.

"Severus would be unbearable at it."

"That's a no?"

"That's a very loud no."

He laughed so hard he almost dropped his noodles.

I leaned toward him.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Please."

His kiss was warm and a little uncertain. I caught his collar and kissed him again, until he stopped looking as though I'd only done it to cheer him up.

"I'm still glad you came," he said.

"So am I. And I still want my date."

"Saturday."

"Saturday."

When we reached home, we left the rest of the evening private. We didn't pretend the ruined reservation was a secret victory; it was a disappointment we'd handled together.

The morning after the emergency, Steven stopped by with news of the damaged windshield. Pearl had spoken to the driver and arranged to handle the repair through the people responsible for the accident. Greg had offered a ride to the repair shop but didn't volunteer to pay every expense as though he alone had caused it.

"You were right to call," Greg told Steven.

Steven looked worried.

"Sorry I ruined your night."

"You didn't ruin it," I said. "The date was interrupted. That's different."

Greg nodded.

"We were disappointed. And we made another plan. I can love you and still wish I'd had a quiet dinner."

Steven considered that.

"Okay."

He gave his father a quick hug, then went to meet the others.

After he left, Greg turned to me.

"Was that too much?"

"No. You told the truth without making Steven responsible for our feelings."

He smiled.

"I'm learning."

We checked the reservation for the next evening and wrote down what time we actually needed to leave. It felt absurdly satisfying. Not heroic. Not a lesson that solved family emergencies forever. Just a plan that belonged to us.

Saturday arrived. We showed up on time. The server remembered us and grinned when Greg solemnly requested water for two people who intended to actually drink it.

Our food arrived hot.

Halfway through dinner Greg checked his phone, then turned it face down after confirming no one needed him.

"You're allowed to relax," I whispered.

"I'm learning."

I smiled.

The date wasn't perfect. He spilled sauce on his shirt, and I laughed at the wrong moment. But we stayed until dessert, then walked along the repaired part of the boardwalk.

This time the only thing we had to rescue was a napkin caught in the wind.
